dataset.dataset_name: HydroSHEDS Watershed Boundaries and River Network
dataset.citation: Lehner, B. et al. (2008). New global hydrography derived from spaceborne elevation data. Eos, Transactions AGU, 89(10), 93-94.
dataset.preprocessing_notes: Use HydroBASINS level 8-10 for sub-watershed delineation context. Stream order used as a primary RWH site-type discriminator: first/second-order streams suit check dams and gully plugs; third/fourth-order streams suit percolation tanks; larger streams suit small dams. Kumar et al. (2018) and Singh et al. (2016) use stream order as a primary MCDA criterion.
dataset.limitations: Derived from 3-arc-second SRTM; misses ephemeral channels in flat arid terrain. Resolution insufficient for first-order gully mapping. Not for: Detailed gully morphometry; flash flood routing
dataset.description: Composite SCS curve-number runoff potential surface combining land-cover and hydrologic soil group.

Reconciled from 3 evidence unit(s) (weighted median, tier×claim_basis). Global {'opt_high': 0.25}; uncertainty ±60% from spread.
Reconciled from 1 evidence unit(s) (weighted median, tier×claim_basis). Global {'opt_low': 0.9}; uncertainty ±20% from spread.

t2_consumers.justification: High runoff depth is simultaneously a flood hazard indicator AND the primary measure of water harvesting opportunity. Terencio et al. (2017) weight overflood risk as a suitability barrier. Abd-el-Kader et al. (2023) and Ahmad et al. (2024) explicitly target high-runoff zones as RWH sites for flood-risk adaptation. Shared variable - used in risk (flood hazard) and opportunity space (RWH potential).
